title: The History of Interactive Computing
excerpt: From Project Whirlwind through the DEC legacy: the early days of interactive computing
content_html:
How computing escaped batch processing, and became personal.
Telling the story through the machines that made it happen.

Most people will mention ENIAC or perhaps the IBM System/360 as examples of early computers. Room-filling machines fed by punch cards, producing payroll runs and scientific calculations. Yes, that was a big part of the story — but it is not our story. The computers we actually use in our daily lives escaped very early on from that path.

Alongside the mainframes, a different strand of computing was taking shape. Where you could use the computer as a tool you could sit down with and interact with. Where you didn't wait hours for a batch job to come back. This is the strand that led to Windows, Linux, Android, the smartphone in your pocket. And to the microcontroller in your dishwasher.

This page is an introduction to that story. It covers the key machines and some of the people. It wants to tell where our computers, and the fundamental ideas behind them, came from.

We admit: this is our perspective. We're Obsolescence Guaranteed, and our goal is to relive these machines hands-on, through the replicas we make of them. We apologise for any oversight or bias. We can't help it, we like our bias.

Prologue: Alan Turing

Before computers, there was the question: what is computation? In 1936, Alan Turing, then a 24-year-old Cambridge mathematician, answered this with a thought experiment. An imaginary machine that could read and write symbols on an infinite tape, following simple rules. The "Universal Turing Machine" could, in principle, perform any calculation that any computer ever could. It was a purely theoretical construct, but defined the boundary of what was possible.

A decade later, Turing was at Bletchley Park, building real machines to break the German Enigma cipher. The Bombes (and later the Colossus) were special-purpose devices, but proved that electronic computing was practical. Turing himself went on to design the ACE (Automatic Computing Engine) at the National Physical Laboratory, one of the first stored-program computers.

Turing's influence on the interactive computing story is fundamental. He showed that a machine could be general-purpose. Not just a calculator, but a tool for thinking.

Turing's ideas were not theoretical. The Pilot ACE, built at the National Physical Laboratory in 1950, was the fastest computer in the world: processing at around 1 MHz, a phenomenal speed for its time. And in 1950, Turing published another seminal paper — "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" — which asked a deceptively simple question: Can machines think? He proposed the Imitation Game, now known as the Turing Test. That question is still unanswered, but interactive computing is what made it worth asking in the first place.

1. Project Whirlwind — The First Interactive Computer

In 1945, the United States Navy asked MIT to build a better flight simulator. They wanted a machine that could model an aircraft in real time, calculating aerodynamic forces fast enough that a pilot could fly it by feel. This was a completely insane request. No computer had ever been built to work at human speed. It became a very successful failure.

Jay Forrester, the young MIT engineer put in charge, did not know this was impossible. He built Whirlwind. Running in 1951, was a revelation. It had a CRT display, you could watch it draw in vectors. It had a light pen, switches and buttons for direct input: the first computer designed to interact with a human being in real time. Every other computer of the era ran batch jobs: hand over your stack of punch cards and come back later. Whirlwind sat there and talked back to you.

Along the way, Forrester and his team invented magnetic core memory. Ferrite rings threaded with wires could hold data (actually, even without power). Core memory remained the dominant random-access memory technology for two decades, and is still used in some spacecraft today. It was born because vacuum tube memory kept failing in Whirlwind, and Forrester needed something reliable.

Whirlwind was a beast: 12,500 vacuum tubes, consuming 150 kW of power, yet managing only 20,000 operations per second. But within the project, something smaller and more significant was taking shape. The Memory Test Computer (MTC) was built to test Forrester's new core memory — and one of the engineers working on it was a young MIT graduate named Ken Olsen. The MTC taught Olsen everything he would later need to build DEC.

Whirlwind's child, the SAGE air defense system, pushed interactive computing even further. SAGE operators sat in front of large CRT displays and used light guns to point at aircraft blips — a direct ancestor of the mouse and every touchscreen that followed.

Whirlwind never succeeded flight simulator role; it was redirected to airspace defence, listening to rader stations and directing interceptor planes. That led directly to the SAGE air defense system. More importantly, it created a generation of engineers at MIT's Lincoln Laboratory who knew, from experience, that computers could do something far more interesting than batch processing.

2. TX-0 — The Transistor Arrives

Whirlwind proved that interactive computing was possible, but filled a largish building and consumed 150 kW of power. The next step was to make it smaller, cheaper, and more accessible. That meant replacing vacuum tubes with transistors.

The TX-0 ("Transistorized Experimental computer zero," affectionately called "tixo") was built at Lincoln Lab between 1955 and 1956. It was the first fully transistorized computer, using around 3,600 Philco surface-barrier transistors. It had a then-huge 64K of 18-bit words of core memory — and, crucially, it had a console. You could sit down at the TX-0 and interact with it directly.

This was the machine that MIT's Tech Model Railroad Club discovered. The TMRC members were already used to building complex signaling systems for their model trains, and when they got access to the TX-0, they found a new kind of playground. They wrote programs, experimented with the display, and pushed the machine in directions its designers had never imagined. They were the first "hackers" — the word already existed in the TMRC to describe an elaborate, creative prank or project — and they brought that ethos to computing.

The word "hacker" did not originate with computers. In the TMRC, a "hack" was an inventive, often playful solution to a technical challenge — wiring a complex signaling system for model trains was a hack. When the club members transferred that mindset to the TX-0, the word found its true home. Hacker still carries that original meaning: not a vandal, but a creative problem-solver who loves the machine.

In a way, the TX-0 was never meant to be more than a stepping stone. It was built as a test platform for the much larger TX-2, a 36-bit machine designed by Wesley Clark. When MIT got its first PDP-1 in 1960, the TX-0 was quietly retired — eventually given away to a museum. Its legacy was not the machine itself, but the generation of engineers and programmers it trained.

Ken Olsen, an MIT engineer who had worked on Whirlwind's memory test computer, directed the construction of the TX-0. He saw where this was going: computers could be personal tools.

3. Digital Equipment Corporation

In 1957, Olsen and Harlan Anderson, both from MIT's Lincoln Lab, decided to start a company. They had $70,000 in venture capital from Georges Doriot's American Research and Development Corporation; one of the first venture capital deals in history. They set up shop in an old nineteenth-century mill building at 146 Main Street in Maynard, Massachusetts.

The company name was a careful choice. In 1957, "computer" was what IBM made — giant, intimidating machines for corporate data centers. No venture capitalist would fund another computer company. So Olsen and Anderson called it Digital Equipment Corporation: "Digital" sounded safe, "Equipment" sounded industrial, and "Computer" was not in the name.

Their first products were logic modules for testing other systems. But Olsen had something bigger in mind. The TX-0 had been followed by the TX-2, a larger 36-bit machine designed by Wesley Clark. Olsen took the lessons of the TX-0 and TX-2 and asked: what if we could make a machine that brought interactive computing out of the lab and into the world?

Olsen would go on to become one of computing's most quotable figures. His most famous line — "There is no reason for any individual to have a computer in his home" (1977) — is almost always taken out of context. He was referring to computers programmed to control household appliances, not the personal computers that were just emerging. Olsen himself had a PDP-11 at home. The remark haunted him for the rest of his career, but it reflects how even the most visionary leaders struggled to predict where interactive computing would go next.

4. PDP-1 — The One That Started It All

In 1959, DEC announced the PDP-1 — the Programmed Data Processor-1. It cost $120,000, about a tenth of the price of an IBM mainframe. It had 4,096 words of 18-bit core memory, 27 instructions, and a central processor built from about 2,700 transistors. Compared to the room-filling IBM machines of the era, it looked like a toy. Only 54 were ever built, but those 54 machines really did change the world.

The PDP-1 had something no IBM machine had: a Type 30 display. It was a converted radar tube. The display took bits directly from the processor's I/O register as X/Y coordinates and drew them on the phosphor screen. It was the simplest possible graphics subsystem. It required no graphics memory, but that meant images had to be redrawn constantly. Still, it was exactly what interactive computing needed.

Spacewar!

In 1962, a group of MIT students — Steve Russell, Martin Graetz, and Wayne Wiitanen — programmed a game on the PDP-1. Two spaceships, controlled by separate sets of switches, fired torpedoes at each other while orbiting a star. They called it Spacewar! It was the first digital video game.

Spacewar! had gravity, thrust mechanics, and a star that would pull you in and destroy you if you weren't careful. It also had the first ever video game controller: a pair of custom switch boxes built by a fellow student, Alan Kotok, who got the parts list from DEC itself. The game was distributed for free, and every PDP-1 site eventually had a copy. It was the first viral piece of software.

The PDP-1 was also the first computer to perform music in public. At MIT's 1963 Science Open House, the Harmony Music Compiler played melodies through a radio speaker wired to the machine's output register. It was an early beginning of computer music — and proof that even with 4K of memory, you could make art.

Where "Hacker" Came From

The MIT PDP-1 community — many of them from the TMRC — took the word "hacker" from the model railroad club and applied it to programming. A hack was an elegant, inventive solution. The PDP-1 was the perfect machine for hacks: simple enough to understand entirely, interactive enough to give instant feedback, and limited enough to demand creativity.

At a time when IBM programmers wrote code, submitted it to a keypunch operator, and got results a day later, PDP-1 hackers sat at the console, toggled in instructions, and watched the results right now. This immediacy was revolutionary. It changed what people thought computers could be.

Firsts Too Numerous to List

The PDP-1 spawned an astonishing number of software firsts. The first text editors. Almost-the-first interactive debugger (DDT, the Dynamic Debugging Technique). The first time-sharing operating systems, allowing multiple users to work simultaneously. Peter Deutsch, a high school student, ported Lisp to the PDP-1 and along the way invented the read-eval-print loop — the REPL that is now the foundation of Python, Ruby, and every interactive programming environment. But the PDP-1, first and foremost, is the birthplace of democoding and gaming:

5. PDP-8 — Glorious Minimalism

The PDP-1 had proven that interactive computing was commercially viable. But DEC realized that to reach a broader market, they needed a machine cheap enough for a single lab or factory floor. So they stripped the PDP-1 concept down to its bare essence.

The PDP-8, introduced in 1965, was the PDP-1's 18-bit architecture shrunk to 12 bits. The instruction set went from 27 to just 8. Memory was 4,096 12-bit words, and the programmer could only directly address 128 words at a time — everything else required page-switching tricks. It cost under $20,000, making it the first computer that an individual department could buy without corporate approval.

DEC thought the PDP-8 would be an industrial controller. Open the valve when pressure gets too high. Stop the heater when temperature rises. They had no idea they were about to invent the personal computer.

DEC's chief engineer, Gordon Bell, called the PDP-8 "the Model T of computing" — and the comparison is apt. Just as Ford's assembly line had made cars affordable, the PDP-8 made computers accessible. And just as the Model T spawned an entire industry of parts and services, the PDP-8 created the minicomputer ecosystem.

The PDP-8's OS/8 operating system was the direct ancestor of CP/M, which in turn was the direct ancestor of MS-DOS. The software DNA of every PC traces back through this lineage. And OS/8 was running on a machine that fit in a rack cabinet, with 4K of memory, in 1968.

Remarkably, the PDP-8 also ran TSS/8, a time-sharing operating system that gave four simultaneous users access to the machine. On a computer with 8 instructions and 4K words of memory. If that sounds impossible, well — that is precisely the point. The PDP-8 forced programmers to be geniuses because it gave them nothing else to work with.

Over 50,000 PDP-8s were sold during its lifetime. It is the prototype/forefather of the personal computer, and of microcontrollers as well.

6. PDP-10 — The mainframe that was actually fun to use

While the PDP-8 was conquering the low end, DEC was working on something entirely different at the high end. The PDP-6 of 1964 had introduced a 36-bit architecture with a rich instruction set that now feels completely alien to modern programmers. But the PDP-6 was unreliable. When DEC got it right with the PDP-10 (KA10, 1968), the result was unlike anything else in computing.

The PDP-10 was a mainframe — it was big, it was expensive (over $100,000), and it was powerful. But unlike other mainframes of the era, it was designed for interactive use. No batch processing. You sat at a terminal and the machine answered you. That was what made the PDP-10 special.

The MIT AI Lab and ITS

At MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the PDP-10 ran an operating system called ITS — the Incompatible Timesharing System. ITS was a hacker's paradise: no passwords, no security. But anyone on the early ARPANET could log in. And they did.

ITS was where Emacs was born (Richard Stallman, 1976). Where MacLisp grew up, pioneering much of modern programming language design. Where Shrdlu — the first AI program that could understand a three-dimensional world and obey English commands — dazzled visitors. Where Mazewar became the first networked multiplayer first-person shooter, connecting PDP-10s across the emerging ARPANET.

It is not an exaggeration to say that modern computer science was forged on the PDP-10. The free software movement began here, with Stallman's reaction to the commercialization of the hacker community. PDP-10s dominated the early ARPANET. And by way of trivia, Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote the first Microsoft BASIC on a Harvard PDP-10, using an 8080 emulator they had written themselves. Open Source and Microsoft were born on the same system!

The PDP-10 also witnessed the very first computer worm. In the early 1970s, a program called Creeper crawled across the ARPANET, displaying "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!" on connected terminals. Another program, Reaper, was unleashed to hunt it down.

Only about 1,500 PDP-10s were ever sold, but their cultural impact is immeasurable. DEC cancelled the line in 1983, killed internally by the success of its own VAX architecture. But the spirit of the PDP-10 lives on in hacker culture.

7. PDP-11 — Defining Normal

In 1970, DEC launched a machine that would change everything. The PDP-11 was a radical break. It was a 16-bit machine with an orthogonal instruction set that made it far easier to program than anything before it. It had eight general-purpose registers (later models had more). It introduced the Unibus, a standardized bus that made adding peripherals simple. And the design scaled up from a tiny 4K embedded controller to a system with 8 megabytes that could rival mainframes — a scale factor of 2,000.

The design was so elegant that every major microprocessor architecture that came after — the Intel x86, the Motorola 68000 — was visibly shaped by it. The 68000's register set, the x86's addressing modes, the very idea of what a CPU should look like: the PDP-11 defined it.

Where Unix Grew Up

In 1970, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs ported their experimental operating system — Unix — to the PDP-11/20. It was the first machine Unix ran on as a named operating system. Over the next decade, Unix and the PDP-11 evolved together. The C programming language was designed specifically to be efficient on the PDP-11's architecture. The abstract machine that C targets, to this day, is a PDP-11 in its fundamental assumptions.

The PDP-11's influence is even visible in the syntax of C itself. The close relationship between arrays and pointers in C — the fact that array[i] is equivalent to *(array + i) — is not an accident of language design. It reflects the PDP-11's architecture, where memory addressing was uniform and efficient. C was not designed for an abstract machine; it was designed for the PDP-11.

The Unix source code for the PDP-11 contains one of the most famous comments in programming history. In the I/O driver for the 11/20, Ken Thompson wrote: "You are not expected to understand this". It was a joke about the complexity of the interrupt system, but it became legendary.

When you open a terminal on a modern Linux or macOS system, you are in a direct line of descent from a programmer sitting at a PDP-11 in 1971. The file system hierarchy, the pipe operator, the shell itself — all of it was invented on the PDP-11.

The Road Not Taken — RSX-11

But Unix was not the only operating system on the PDP-11, and in fact it was DEC's least favorite. The company's own RSX-11M was a groundbreaking multi-user, real-time OS that feels utterly different from Unix. But its integrated development environment, its seamless multitasking, its approach to resource management — RSX was an alternative vision of computing that could have won. Easily.

Here is where the story takes a strange turn. When Microsoft decided to break with the MS-DOS past in the late 1980s, Dave Cutler, the lead architect of RSX-11M (and later of DEC's VMS), was tasked with building a new operating system from scratch. That became Windows NT. Its kernel design, its I/O model, and its structured exception handling all bear the marks of the PDP-11 RSX heritage. So: the other half of the modern desktop, the non-Unix half, also traces back to the PDP-11.

Over 600,000 PDP-11s were sold. They were used in laboratories, factories, universities, telephone exchanges, and spacecraft. The top-of-the-line PDP-11/70 pushed performance further with a second MASSBUS interface, capable of transferring data at 4 megabytes per second — breathtaking speed in 1975. The architecture remained in production for over 25 years. When you use any modern computer — PC, Mac, or Linux workstation — you are running on decisions made by the PDP-11's designers in the late 1960s.

8. The ARPANET — Where It All Connected

By the late 1960s, the problem was not computing power — it was isolation. Research labs across the United States had powerful interactive computers, but each was an island. If you worked on a PDP-10 at MIT's AI Lab and wanted to use a program running on a machine at Stanford, you got in your car.

The answer came from the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), a Pentagon agency that had been funding much of this computer science research. In 1968, ARPA issued a request for proposals to build an experimental packet-switched network. The contract went to Bolt, Beranek and Newman (BBN), a Cambridge, Massachusetts firm founded by two MIT professors. BBN had deep DEC expertise — they owned several PDP-1s and PDP-10s, and knew exactly how to make computers talk to each other.

The device that made it work was the IMP — the Interface Message Processor. It was a rugged minicomputer (initially a Honeywell DDP-516) that sat between a site's main computer and the telephone lines. Its job was to receive messages from the local machine, chop them into packets, and route them across the network to the destination. The IMP was the first purpose-built network router, and its software was written by a BBN team that included several former MIT hackers.

The first four ARPANET nodes went live in late 1969: UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. By 1971 there were fifteen. MIT joined early, and its PDP-10 running ITS became one of the network's most popular destinations — the magical place where the hacker ethos met the network.

In 1971, BBN engineer Ray Tomlinson invented email. He chose the @ symbol to separate the user's name from the machine's name because it was already on the keyboard and "made sense." Email would become the early ARPANET's killer app — and the @ sign is still with us.

1972: The Demo That Changed Everything

In October 1972, ARPA organized a public demonstration at the International Conference on Computer Communication in Washington, D.C. For three days, attendees could sit at one of 40 terminals connected to computers at 10 sites across the country — clattering Teletypes and sleek new CRT terminals — to connect with computers across the country. They could log into MIT's PDP-10, run programs on the Stanford AI Lab's machine, send messages to BBN's PDP-10 in Cambridge. The network worked. And people saw it work.

This was the moment the internet went from research project to an inevitability. The terminals at the 1972 demo were connected through IMPs that routed their traffic through leased telephone lines, entirely automatically. The technology was self-organizing — an IMP would announce its presence, learn about its neighbors, and within seconds the entire network knew about it. That design principle, refined over decades, is still how the internet works today.

The ARPANET grew rapidly through the 1970s. PDP-10s were its early backbone — the machines that ran the early network services, hosted the first email servers, and formed the kernel of what would become the internet. By 1977, the network had evolved into a web spanning the continent.

Currently, we're building a replica of the IMP as part of a larger ARPANET Reconstruction Project, aiming to recreate the 1972-73 network to surf on. It is the final piece of the puzzle, linking all the machines in this story together.

Looking back

The story of interactive computing is not just about hardware. It's also about a shift in what people believed computers were for. Whirlwind proved that a computer could respond to a human in real time. The TX-0 and the MIT hackers proved that interactive access bred creativity. DEC built a business around making computers personal tools rather than institutional mainframes.

Each of these machines built on the ones before it, but they were not a smooth progression. The PDP-8 was a deliberate reduction, but made computing far more accessible. It is the seed from which early personal computers and microcontrollers all come from. The PDP-10 moved into mainframe territory, but with a hacker's heart. The birthplace of modern software, though the hardware itself actually turned out to be a dead end. And the PDP-11 was a rethinking from the ground up that got so many things right that it is the first 'normal' computer - it defined what we use today.

By the early 1980s, the microprocessor had absorbed the lessons of all these machines. The interactive computing battle was won.

But there is still something special about experiencing these forefather machines. To toggle in a bootstrap on a PDP-8 front panel and watch the Blinkenlights as it loads a paper tape. To sit at a PDP-1 console and type in 12 lines of assembly code that draws a circle on a radar tube. To log into ITS on a PDP-10 and realize you are using the same operating system that Richard Stallman used when he invented Emacs, and which carried the earliest AI.

That is why our replica community exists. These machines cannot just be dead artifacts in museums — they should be experienced hands-on to understand computer history. A museum may show you history. A replica lets you live it.

The display took bits directly from the processor's I/O register as X/Y coordinates and drew them on the phosphor screen. It was the simplest possible graphics subsystem. It required no graphics memory, but that meant images had to be redrawn constantly. Still, it was exactly what interactive computing needed. Spacewar! In 1962, a group of MIT students — Steve Russell, Martin Graetz, and Wayne Wiitanen — programmed a game on the PDP-1. Two spaceships, controlled by separate sets of switches, fired torpedoes at each other while orbiting a star. They called it Spacewar! It was the first digital video game. Spacewar! had gravity, thrust mechanics, and a star that would pull you in and destroy you if you weren't careful. It also had the first ever video game controller: a pair of custom switch boxes built by a fellow student, Alan Kotok, who got the parts list from DEC itself. The game was distributed for free, and every PDP-1 site eventually had a copy. It was the first viral piece of software. The PDP-1 was also the first computer to perform music in public. At MIT's 1963 Science Open House, the Harmony Music Compiler played melodies through a radio speaker wired to the machine's output register. It was an early beginning of computer music — and proof that even with 4K of memory, you could make art. Where "Hacker" Came From The MIT PDP-1 community — many of them from the TMRC — took the word "hacker" from the model railroad club and applied it to programming. A hack was an elegant, inventive solution. The PDP-1 was the perfect machine for hacks: simple enough to understand entirely, interactive enough to give instant feedback, and limited enough to demand creativity. At a time when IBM programmers wrote code, submitted it to a keypunch operator, and got results a day later, PDP-1 hackers sat at the console, toggled in instructions, and watched the results right now. This immediacy was revolutionary. It changed what people thought computers could be. Firsts Too Numerous to List The PDP-1 spawned an astonishing number of software firsts. The first text editors. Almost-the-first interactive debugger (DDT, the Dynamic Debugging Technique). The first time-sharing operating systems, allowing multiple users to work simultaneously. Peter Deutsch, a high school student, ported Lisp to the PDP-1 and along the way invented the read-eval-print loop — the REPL that is now the foundation of Python, Ruby, and every interactive programming environment. But the PDP-1, first and foremost, is the birthplace of democoding and gaming: 5. PDP-8 — Glorious Minimalism The PDP-1 had proven that interactive computing was commercially viable. But DEC realized that to reach a broader market, they needed a machine cheap enough for a single lab or factory floor. So they stripped the PDP-1 concept down to its bare essence. The PDP-8, introduced in 1965, was the PDP-1's 18-bit architecture shrunk to 12 bits. The instruction set went from 27 to just 8. Memory was 4,096 12-bit words, and the programmer could only directly address 128 words at a time — everything else required page-switching tricks. It cost under $20,000, making it the first computer that an individual department could buy without corporate approval. DEC thought the PDP-8 would be an industrial controller. Open the valve when pressure gets too high. Stop the heater when temperature rises. They had no idea they were about to invent the personal computer. DEC's chief engineer, Gordon Bell, called the PDP-8 "the Model T of computing" — and the comparison is apt. Just as Ford's assembly line had made cars affordable, the PDP-8 made computers accessible. And just as the Model T spawned an entire industry of parts and services, the PDP-8 created the minicomputer ecosystem. The PDP-8's OS/8 operating system was the direct ancestor of CP/M, which in turn was the direct ancestor of MS-DOS. The software DNA of every PC traces back through this lineage. And OS/8 was running on a machine that fit in a rack cabinet, with 4K of memory, in 1968. Remarkably, the PDP-8 also ran TSS/8, a time-sharing operating system that gave four simultaneous users access to the machine. On a computer with 8 instructions and 4K words of memory. If that sounds impossible, well — that is precisely the point. The PDP-8 forced programmers to be geniuses because it gave them nothing else to work with. Over 50,000 PDP-8s were sold during its lifetime. It is the prototype/forefather of the personal computer, and of microcontrollers as well. 6. PDP-10 — The mainframe that was actually fun to use While the PDP-8 was conquering the low end, DEC was working on something entirely different at the high end. The PDP-6 of 1964 had introduced a 36-bit architecture with a rich instruction set that now feels completely alien to modern programmers. But the PDP-6 was unreliable. When DEC got it right with the PDP-10 (KA10, 1968), the result was unlike anything else in computing. The PDP-10 was a mainframe — it was big, it was expensive (over $100,000), and it was powerful. But unlike other mainframes of the era, it was designed for interactive use. No batch processing. You sat at a terminal and the machine answered you. That was what made the PDP-10 special. The MIT AI Lab and ITS At MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the PDP-10 ran an operating system called ITS — the Incompatible Timesharing System. ITS was a hacker's paradise: no passwords, no security. But anyone on the early ARPANET could log in. And they did. ITS was where Emacs was born (Richard Stallman, 1976). Where MacLisp grew up, pioneering much of modern programming language design. Where Shrdlu — the first AI program that could understand a three-dimensional world and obey English commands — dazzled visitors. Where Mazewar became the first networked multiplayer first-person shooter, connecting PDP-10s across the emerging ARPANET. It is not an exaggeration to say that modern computer science was forged on the PDP-10. The free software movement began here, with Stallman's reaction to the commercialization of the hacker community. PDP-10s dominated the early ARPANET. And by way of trivia, Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote the first Microsoft BASIC on a Harvard PDP-10, using an 8080 emulator they had written themselves. Open Source and Microsoft were born on the same system! The PDP-10 also witnessed the very first computer worm. In the early 1970s, a program called Creeper crawled across the ARPANET, displaying "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!" on connected terminals. Another program, Reaper, was unleashed to hunt it down. Only about 1,500 PDP-10s were ever sold, but their cultural impact is immeasurable. DEC cancelled the line in 1983, killed internally by the success of its own VAX architecture. But the spirit of the PDP-10 lives on in hacker culture. 7. PDP-11 — Defining Normal In 1970, DEC launched a machine that would change everything. The PDP-11 was a radical break. It was a 16-bit machine with an orthogonal instruction set that made it far easier to program than anything before it. It had eight general-purpose registers (later models had more). It introduced the Unibus, a standardized bus that made adding peripherals simple. And the design scaled up from a tiny 4K embedded controller to a system with 8 megabytes that could rival mainframes — a scale factor of 2,000. The design was so elegant that every major microprocessor architecture that came after — the Intel x86, the Motorola 68000 — was visibly shaped by it. The 68000's register set, the x86's addressing modes, the very idea of what a CPU should look like: the PDP-11 defined it. Where Unix Grew Up In 1970, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs ported their experimental operating system — Unix — to the PDP-11/20. It was the first machine Unix ran on as a named operating system. Over the next decade, Unix and the PDP-11 evolved together. The C programming language was designed specifically to be efficient on the PDP-11's architecture. The abstract machine that C targets, to this day, is a PDP-11 in its fundamental assumptions. The PDP-11's influence is even visible in the syntax of C itself. The close relationship between arrays and pointers in C — the fact that array[i] is equivalent to *(array + i) — is not an accident of language design. It reflects the PDP-11's architecture, where memory addressing was uniform and efficient. C was not designed for an abstract machine; it was designed for the PDP-11. The Unix source code for the PDP-11 contains one of the most famous comments in programming history. In the I/O driver for the 11/20, Ken Thompson wrote: "You are not expected to understand this". It was a joke about the complexity of the interrupt system, but it became legendary. When you open a terminal on a modern Linux or macOS system, you are in a direct line of descent from a programmer sitting at a PDP-11 in 1971. The file system hierarchy, the pipe operator, the shell itself — all of it was invented on the PDP-11. The Road Not Taken — RSX-11 But Unix was not the only operating system on the PDP-11, and in fact it was DEC's least favorite. The company's own RSX-11M was a groundbreaking multi-user, real-time OS that feels utterly different from Unix. But its integrated development environment, its seamless multitasking, its approach to resource management — RSX was an alternative vision of computing that could have won. Easily. Here is where the story takes a strange turn. When Microsoft decided to break with the MS-DOS past in the late 1980s, Dave Cutler, the lead architect of RSX-11M (and later of DEC's VMS), was tasked with building a new operating system from scratch. That became Windows NT. Its kernel design, its I/O model, and its structured exception handling all bear the marks of the PDP-11 RSX heritage. So: the other half of the modern desktop, the non-Unix half, also traces back to the PDP-11. Over 600,000 PDP-11s were sold. They were used in laboratories, factories, universities, telephone exchanges, and spacecraft. The top-of-the-line PDP-11/70 pushed performance further with a second MASSBUS interface, capable of transferring data at 4 megabytes per second — breathtaking speed in 1975. The architecture remained in production for over 25 years. When you use any modern computer — PC, Mac, or Linux workstation — you are running on decisions made by the PDP-11's designers in the late 1960s. 8. The ARPANET — Where It All Connected By the late 1960s, the problem was not computing power — it was isolation. Research labs across the United States had powerful interactive computers, but each was an island. If you worked on a PDP-10 at MIT's AI Lab and wanted to use a program running on a machine at Stanford, you got in your car. The answer came from the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA), a Pentagon agency that had been funding much of this computer science research. In 1968, ARPA issued a request for proposals to build an experimental packet-switched network. The contract went to Bolt, Beranek and Newman (BBN), a Cambridge, Massachusetts firm founded by two MIT professors. BBN had deep DEC expertise — they owned several PDP-1s and PDP-10s, and knew exactly how to make computers talk to each other. The device that made it work was the IMP — the Interface Message Processor. It was a rugged minicomputer (initially a Honeywell DDP-516) that sat between a site's main computer and the telephone lines. Its job was to receive messages from the local machine, chop them into packets, and route them across the network to the destination. The IMP was the first purpose-built network router, and its software was written by a BBN team that included several former MIT hackers. The first four ARPANET nodes went live in late 1969: UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. By 1971 there were fifteen. MIT joined early, and its PDP-10 running ITS became one of the network's most popular destinations — the magical place where the hacker ethos met the network. In 1971, BBN engineer Ray Tomlinson invented email. He chose the @ symbol to separate the user's name from the machine's name because it was already on the keyboard and "made sense." Email would become the early ARPANET's killer app — and the @ sign is still with us. 1972: The Demo That Changed Everything In October 1972, ARPA organized a public demonstration at the International Conference on Computer Communication in Washington, D.C. For three days, attendees could sit at one of 40 terminals connected to computers at 10 sites across the country — clattering Teletypes and sleek new CRT terminals — to connect with computers across the country. They could log into MIT's PDP-10, run programs on the Stanford AI Lab's machine, send messages to BBN's PDP-10 in Cambridge. The network worked. And people saw it work. This was the moment the internet went from research project to an inevitability. The terminals at the 1972 demo were connected through IMPs that routed their traffic through leased telephone lines, entirely automatically. The technology was self-organizing — an IMP would announce its presence, learn about its neighbors, and within seconds the entire network knew about it. That design principle, refined over decades, is still how the internet works today. The ARPANET grew rapidly through the 1970s. PDP-10s were its early backbone — the machines that ran the early network services, hosted the first email servers, and formed the kernel of what would become the internet. By 1977, the network had evolved into a web spanning the continent. Currently, we're building a replica of the IMP as part of a larger ARPANET Reconstruction Project, aiming to recreate the 1972-73 network to surf on. It is the final piece of the puzzle, linking all the machines in this story together. Looking back The story of interactive computing is not just about hardware. It's also about a shift in what people believed computers were for. Whirlwind proved that a computer could respond to a human in real time. The TX-0 and the MIT hackers proved that interactive access bred creativity. DEC built a business around making computers personal tools rather than institutional mainframes. Each of these machines built on the ones before it, but they were not a smooth progression. The PDP-8 was a deliberate reduction, but made computing far more accessible. It is the seed from which early personal computers and microcontrollers all come from. The PDP-10 moved into mainframe territory, but with a hacker's heart. The birthplace of modern software, though the hardware itself actually turned out to be a dead end. And the PDP-11 was a rethinking from the ground up that got so many things right that it is the first 'normal' computer - it defined what we use today. By the early 1980s, the microprocessor had absorbed the lessons of all these machines. The interactive computing battle was won. But there is still something special about experiencing these forefather machines. To toggle in a bootstrap on a PDP-8 front panel and watch the Blinkenlights as it loads a paper tape. To sit at a PDP-1 console and type in 12 lines of assembly code that draws a circle on a radar tube. To log into ITS on a PDP-10 and realize you are using the same operating system that Richard Stallman used when he invented Emacs, and which carried the earliest AI. That is why our replica community exists. These machines cannot just be dead artifacts in museums — they should be experienced hands-on to understand computer history. A museum may show you history. A replica lets you live it. Back to the main site

blocks.html_en: Most people will mention ENIAC or perhaps the IBM System/360 as examples of early computers. Room-filling machines fed by punch cards, producing payroll runs and scientific calculations. Yes, that was a big part of the story — but it is not our story. The computers we actually use in our daily lives escaped very early on from that path.

blocks.html_en: Prologue: Alan Turing

sentences.en: Prologue: Alan Turing
sentences.zh: 序言：阿兰·图灵

blocks.html_en: Before computers, there was the question: what is computation? In 1936, Alan Turing, then a 24-year-old Cambridge mathematician, answered this with a thought experiment. An imaginary machine that could read and write symbols on an infinite tape, following simple rules. The "Universal Turing Machine" could, in principle, perform any calculation that any computer ever could. It was a purely theoretical construct, but defined the boundary of what was possible.

sentences.en: Before computers, there was the question: what is computation?
sentences.zh: 在计算机出现之前，存在一个问题：什么是计算？

sentences.zh: 1936年，当时24岁的剑桥数学家艾伦·图灵通过一个思想实验回答了这个问题。

blocks.html_en: A decade later, Turing was at Bletchley Park, building real machines to break the German Enigma cipher. The Bombes (and later the Colossus) were special-purpose devices, but proved that electronic computing was practical. Turing himself went on to design the ACE (Automatic Computing Engine) at the National Physical Laboratory, one of the first stored-program computers.

blocks.html_en: Turing's influence on the interactive computing story is fundamental. He showed that a machine could be general-purpose. Not just a calculator, but a tool for thinking.

blocks.html_en: Turing's ideas were not theoretical. The Pilot ACE, built at the National Physical Laboratory in 1950, was the fastest computer in the world: processing at around 1 MHz, a phenomenal speed for its time. And in 1950, Turing published another seminal paper — "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" — which asked a deceptively simple question: Can machines think? He proposed the Imitation Game, now known as the Turing Test. That question is still unanswered, but interactive computing is what made it worth asking in the first place.

blocks.html_en: 1. Project Whirlwind — The First Interactive Computer

sentences.en: Project Whirlwind — The First Interactive Computer
sentences.zh: 旋风计划——第一台交互式计算机

blocks.html_en: In 1945, the United States Navy asked MIT to build a better flight simulator. They wanted a machine that could model an aircraft in real time, calculating aerodynamic forces fast enough that a pilot could fly it by feel. This was a completely insane request. No computer had ever been built to work at human speed. It became a very successful failure.

blocks.html_en: Jay Forrester, the young MIT engineer put in charge, did not know this was impossible. He built Whirlwind. Running in 1951, was a revelation. It had a CRT display, you could watch it draw in vectors. It had a light pen, switches and buttons for direct input: the first computer designed to interact with a human being in real time. Every other computer of the era ran batch jobs: hand over your stack of punch cards and come back later. Whirlwind sat there and talked back to you.

blocks.html_en: Along the way, Forrester and his team invented magnetic core memory. Ferrite rings threaded with wires could hold data (actually, even without power). Core memory remained the dominant random-access memory technology for two decades, and is still used in some spacecraft today. It was born because vacuum tube memory kept failing in Whirlwind, and Forrester needed something reliable.

blocks.html_en: Whirlwind was a beast: 12,500 vacuum tubes, consuming 150 kW of power, yet managing only 20,000 operations per second. But within the project, something smaller and more significant was taking shape. The Memory Test Computer (MTC) was built to test Forrester's new core memory — and one of the engineers working on it was a young MIT graduate named Ken Olsen. blocks.html_en: 2. TX-0 — The Transistor Arrives

sentences.en: TX-0 — The Transistor Arrives
sentences.zh: TX-0 — 晶体管到货

blocks.html_en: Whirlwind proved that interactive computing was possible, but filled a largish building and consumed 150 kW of power. The next step was to make it smaller, cheaper, and more accessible. That meant replacing vacuum tubes with transistors.

sentences.zh: 这意味着用晶体管取代真空管。

blocks.html_en: The TX-0 ("Transistorized Experimental computer zero," affectionately called "tixo") was built at Lincoln Lab between 1955 and 1956. It was the first fully transistorized computer, using around 3,600 Philco surface-barrier transistors. It had a then-huge 64K of 18-bit words of core memory — and, crucially, it had a console. You could sit down at the TX-0 and interact with it directly.

Hacker still carries that original meaning: not a vandal, but a creative problem-solver who loves the machine.

They set up shop in an old nineteenth-century mill building at 146 Main Street in Maynard, Massachusetts.

blocks.html_en: Olsen would go on to become one of computing's most quotable figures. His most famous line — "There is no reason for any individual to have a computer in his home" (1977) — is almost always taken out of context. The remark haunted him for the rest of his career, but it reflects how even the most visionary leaders struggled to predict where interactive computing would go next.

blocks.html_en: 4. PDP-1 — The One That Started It All

sentences.en: PDP-1 — The One That Started It All

blocks.html_en: In 1959, DEC announced the PDP-1 — the Programmed Data Processor-1. It cost $120,000, about a tenth of the price of an IBM mainframe. It had 4,096 words of 18-bit core memory, 27 instructions, and a central processor built from about 2,700 transistors. Compared to the room-filling IBM machines of the era, it looked like a toy. Only 54 were ever built, but those 54 machines really did change the world.

It required no graphics memory, but that meant images had to be redrawn constantly. Still, it was exactly what interactive computing needed.

The PDP-1 was the perfect machine for hacks: simple enough to understand entirely, interactive enough to give instant feedback, and limited enough to demand creativity.

blocks.html_en: The PDP-1 spawned an astonishing number of software firsts. The first text editors. Almost-the-first interactive debugger (DDT, the Dynamic Debugging Technique). The first time-sharing operating systems, allowing multiple users to work simultaneously. But the PDP-1, first and foremost, is the birthplace of democoding and gaming:

sentences.zh: 第一个文本编辑器。

sentences.en: Almost-the-first interactive debugger (DDT, the Dynamic Debugging Technique).
sentences.zh: 几乎第一个交互式调试器（DDT，动态调试技术）。

sentences.en: The first time-sharing operating systems, allowing multiple users to work simultaneously.
sentences.zh: 第一个分时操作系统，允许多个用户同时工作。

sentences.en: Peter Deutsch, a high school student, ported Lisp to the PDP-1 and along the way invented the read-eval-print loop — the REPL that is now the foundation of Python, Ruby, and every interactive programming environment.
sentences.zh: Peter Deutsch，一名高中生，将 Lisp 移植到了 PDP-1，并在此过程中发明了读取-评估-打印循环——REPL，现在是 Python、Ruby 和每个交互式编程环境的基础。

sentences.en: But the PDP-1, first and foremost, is the birthplace of democoding and gaming:
sentences.zh: 但 PDP-1 首先是解码和游戏的诞生地：

blocks.html_en: 5. PDP-8 — Glorious Minimalism

sentences.en: PDP-8 — Glorious Minimalism
sentences.zh: PDP-8 — 光荣的极简主义

blocks.html_en: The PDP-1 had proven that interactive computing was commercially viable. But DEC realized that to reach a broader market, they needed a machine cheap enough for a single lab or factory floor. So they stripped the PDP-1 concept down to its bare essence.

sentences.en: The PDP-1 had proven that interactive computing was commercially viable.
sentences.zh: PDP-1 已经证明交互式计算在商业上是可行的。

sentences.en: But DEC realized that to reach a broader market, they needed a machine cheap enough for a single lab or factory floor.
sentences.zh: 但 DEC 意识到，为了进入更广阔的市场，他们需要一台足够便宜的机器，用于单个实验室或工厂车间。

sentences.en: So they stripped the PDP-1 concept down to its bare essence.
sentences.zh: 因此，他们将 PDP-1 概念剥离至其本质。

blocks.html_en: The PDP-8, introduced in 1965, was the PDP-1's 18-bit architecture shrunk to 12 bits. The instruction set went from 27 to just 8. Memory was 4,096 12-bit words, and the programmer could only directly address 128 words at a time — everything else required page-switching tricks. It cost under $20,000, making it the first computer that an individual department could buy without corporate approval.

sentences.en: The PDP-8, introduced in 1965, was the PDP-1's 18-bit architecture shrunk to 12 bits.
sentences.zh: PDP-8 于 1965 年推出，是将 PDP-1 的 18 位架构缩减为 12 位。

sentences.en: The instruction set went from 27 to just 8.
sentences.zh: 指令集从 27 条减少到 8 条。

sentences.en: Memory was 4,096 12-bit words, and the programmer could only directly address 128 words at a time — everything else required page-switching tricks.
sentences.zh: 内存为 4,096 个 12 位字，程序员一次只能直接寻址 128 个字——其他一切都需要页面切换技巧。

sentences.en: It cost under $20,000, making it the first computer that an individual department could buy without corporate approval.
sentences.zh: 它的价格不到 20,000 美元，使其成为第一台单个部门无需公司批准即可购买的计算机。

blocks.html_en: DEC thought the PDP-8 would be an industrial controller. Open the valve when pressure gets too high. Stop the heater when temperature rises. They had no idea they were about to invent the personal computer.

sentences.en: DEC thought the PDP-8 would be an industrial controller.
sentences.zh: DEC 认为 PDP-8 将是一个工业控制器。

sentences.en: Open the valve when pressure gets too high.
sentences.zh: 当压力过高时打开阀门。

sentences.en: Stop the heater when temperature rises.
sentences.zh: 当温度升高时停止加热器。

sentences.en: They had no idea they were about to invent the personal computer.
sentences.zh: 他们不知道自己即将发明个人计算机。

blocks.html_en: DEC's chief engineer, Gordon Bell, called the PDP-8 "the Model T of computing" — and the comparison is apt. Just as Ford's assembly line had made cars affordable, the PDP-8 made computers accessible. And just as the Model T spawned an entire industry of parts and services, the PDP-8 created the minicomputer ecosystem.

sentences.en: DEC's chief engineer, Gordon Bell, called the PDP-8 "the Model T of computing" — and the comparison is apt.
sentences.zh: DEC 的首席工程师戈登·贝尔 (Gordon Bell) 将 PDP-8 称为“计算领域的 T 型”，这种比较是恰当的。

sentences.en: Just as Ford's assembly line had made cars affordable, the PDP-8 made computers accessible.
sentences.zh: 正如福特的装配线让汽车变得更便宜一样，PDP-8 让计算机变得触手可及。

sentences.en: And just as the Model T spawned an entire industry of parts and services, the PDP-8 created the minicomputer ecosystem.
sentences.zh: 正如 T 型车催生了整个零部件和服务行业一样，PDP-8 创建了小型机生态系统。

blocks.html_en: The PDP-8's OS/8 operating system was the direct ancestor of CP/M, which in turn was the direct ancestor of MS-DOS. The software DNA of every PC traces back through this lineage. And OS/8 was running on a machine that fit in a rack cabinet, with 4K of memory, in 1968.

sentences.en: The PDP-8's OS/8 operating system was the direct ancestor of CP/M, which in turn was the direct ancestor of MS-DOS.
sentences.zh: PDP-8 的 OS/8 操作系统是 CP/M 的直接祖先，而 CP/M 又是 MS-DOS 的直接祖先。

sentences.en: The software DNA of every PC traces back through this lineage.
sentences.zh: 每台 PC 的软件 DNA 都可以追溯到这个血统。

sentences.en: And OS/8 was running on a machine that fit in a rack cabinet, with 4K of memory, in 1968.
sentences.zh: 1968 年，OS/8 运行在一台安装在机架式机箱中、具有 4K 内存的机器上。

blocks.html_en: Remarkably, the PDP-8 also ran TSS/8, a time-sharing operating system that gave four simultaneous users access to the machine. On a computer with 8 instructions and 4K words of memory. If that sounds impossible, well — that is precisely the point. The PDP-8 forced programmers to be geniuses because it gave them nothing else to work with.

sentences.en: Remarkably, the PDP-8 also ran TSS/8, a time-sharing operating system that gave four simultaneous users access to the machine.
sentences.zh: 值得注意的是，PDP-8 还运行 TSS/8，这是一种分时操作系统，可以让四个用户同时访问该机器。

sentences.en: On a computer with 8 instructions and 4K words of memory.
sentences.zh: 在具有 8 条指令和 4K 字内存的计算机上。

sentences.en: If that sounds impossible, well — that is precisely the point.
sentences.zh: 如果这听起来不可能，那么——这正是重点。

sentences.en: The PDP-8 forced programmers to be geniuses because it gave them nothing else to work with.
sentences.zh: PDP-8 迫使程序员成为天才，因为它没有给他们提供其他可以使用的东西。

blocks.html_en: Over 50,000 PDP-8s were sold during its lifetime. It is the prototype/forefather of the personal computer, and of microcontrollers as well.

sentences.en: Over 50,000 PDP-8s were sold during its lifetime.
sentences.zh: PDP-8 在其生命周期内已售出超过 50,000 台。

sentences.en: It is the prototype/forefather of the personal computer, and of microcontrollers as well.
sentences.zh: 它是个人计算机和微控制器的原型/鼻祖。

blocks.html_en: 6. PDP-10 — The mainframe that was actually fun to use

sentences.en: PDP-10 — The mainframe that was actually fun to use
sentences.zh: PDP-10 — 使用起来确实很有趣的主机

blocks.html_en: While the PDP-8 was conquering the low end, DEC was working on something entirely different at the high end. The PDP-6 of 1964 had introduced a 36-bit architecture with a rich instruction set that now feels completely alien to modern programmers. But the PDP-6 was unreliable. When DEC got it right with the PDP-10 (KA10, 1968), the result was unlike anything else in computing.

sentences.en: While the PDP-8 was conquering the low end, DEC was working on something entirely different at the high end.
sentences.zh: 当 PDP-8 征服低端市场时，DEC 正在开发一些完全不同的高端产品。

sentences.en: The PDP-6 of 1964 had introduced a 36-bit architecture with a rich instruction set that now feels completely alien to modern programmers.
sentences.zh: 1964 年的 PDP-6 引入了具有丰富指令集的 36 位架构，但现在对现代程序员来说完全陌生。

sentences.en: But the PDP-6 was unreliable.
sentences.zh: 但 PDP-6 并不可靠。

sentences.en: When DEC got it right with the PDP-10 (KA10, 1968), the result was unlike anything else in computing.
sentences.zh: 当 DEC 正确使用 PDP-10（KA10，1968）时，其结果与计算领域的其他任何结果都不同。

blocks.html_en: The PDP-10 was a mainframe — it was big, it was expensive (over $100,000), and it was powerful. But unlike other mainframes of the era, it was designed for interactive use. No batch processing. You sat at a terminal and the machine answered you. That was what made the PDP-10 special.

sentences.en: The PDP-10 was a mainframe — it was big, it was expensive (over $100,000), and it was powerful.
sentences.zh: PDP-10 是一个大型机——它很大，很昂贵（超过 100,000 美元），而且功能强大。

sentences.en: But unlike other mainframes of the era, it was designed for interactive use.
sentences.zh: 但与同时代的其他大型机不同，它是为交互式使用而设计的。

sentences.en: No batch processing.
sentences.zh: 没有批处理。

sentences.en: You sat at a terminal and the machine answered you.
sentences.zh: 你坐在终端前，机器回答你。

sentences.en: That was what made the PDP-10 special.
sentences.zh: 这就是 PDP-10 的特殊之处。

blocks.html_en: The MIT AI Lab and ITS

sentences.en: The MIT AI Lab and ITS
sentences.zh: 麻省理工学院人工智能实验室和 ITS

blocks.html_en: At MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the PDP-10 ran an operating system called ITS — the Incompatible Timesharing System. ITS was a hacker's paradise: no passwords, no security. But anyone on the early ARPANET could log in. And they did.

sentences.en: At MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the PDP-10 ran an operating system called ITS — the Incompatible Timesharing System.
sentences.zh: 在麻省理工学院的人工智能实验室，PDP-10 运行一个名为 ITS 的操作系统——不兼容分时系统。

sentences.en: ITS was a hacker's paradise: no passwords, no security.
sentences.zh: ITS 是黑客的天堂：没有密码，没有安全保障。

sentences.en: But anyone on the early ARPANET could log in.
sentences.zh: 但早期阿帕网上的任何人都可以登录。

sentences.en: And they did.
sentences.zh: 他们做到了。

blocks.html_en: ITS was where Emacs was born (Richard Stallman, 1976). Where MacLisp grew up, pioneering much of modern programming language design. Where Shrdlu — the first AI program that could understand a three-dimensional world and obey English commands — dazzled visitors. Where Mazewar became the first networked multiplayer first-person shooter, connecting PDP-10s across the emerging ARPANET.

sentences.en: ITS was where Emacs was born (Richard Stallman, 1976).
sentences.zh: ITS 是 Emacs 的诞生地（Richard Stallman，1976）。

sentences.en: Where MacLisp grew up, pioneering much of modern programming language design.
sentences.zh: MacLisp 在这里成长，开创了许多现代编程语言设计的先河。

sentences.en: Where Shrdlu — the first AI program that could understand a three-dimensional world and obey English commands — dazzled visitors.
sentences.zh: Shrdlu——第一个能够理解三维世界并遵守英语命令的人工智能程序——让参观者眼花缭乱。

sentences.en: Where Mazewar became the first networked multiplayer first-person shooter, connecting PDP-10s across the emerging ARPANET.
sentences.zh: Mazewar 成为第一款网络多人第一人称射击游戏，通过新兴的 ARPANET 连接 PDP-10。

blocks.html_en: It is not an exaggeration to say that modern computer science was forged on the PDP-10. The free software movement began here, with Stallman's reaction to the commercialization of the hacker community. PDP-10s dominated the early ARPANET. And by way of trivia, Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote the first Microsoft BASIC on a Harvard PDP-10, using an 8080 emulator they had written themselves. Open Source and Microsoft were born on the same system!

sentences.en: It is not an exaggeration to say that modern computer science was forged on the PDP-10.
sentences.zh: 可以毫不夸张地说，现代计算机科学是在PDP-10上锻造出来的。

sentences.en: The free software movement began here, with Stallman's reaction to the commercialization of the hacker community.
sentences.zh: 自由软件运动始于斯托曼对黑客社区商业化的反应。

sentences.en: PDP-10s dominated the early ARPANET.
sentences.zh: PDP-10 在早期的 ARPANET 中占据主导地位。

sentences.en: And by way of trivia, Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote the first Microsoft BASIC on a Harvard PDP-10, using an 8080 emulator they had written themselves.
sentences.zh: 顺便说一句，比尔·盖茨和保罗·艾伦使用他们自己编写的 8080 模拟器在哈佛 PDP-10 上编写了第一个 Microsoft BASIC。

sentences.en: Open Source and Microsoft were born on the same system!
sentences.zh: 开源和微软诞生在同一个系统上！

blocks.html_en: The PDP-10 also witnessed the very first computer worm. In the early 1970s, a program called Creeper crawled across the ARPANET, displaying "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!" on connected terminals. Another program, Reaper, was unleashed to hunt it down.

sentences.en: The PDP-10 also witnessed the very first computer worm.
sentences.zh: PDP-10 还见证了第一个计算机蠕虫病毒。

sentences.en: In the early 1970s, a program called Creeper crawled across the ARPANET, displaying "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!"
sentences.zh: 20 世纪 70 年代初，一个名为 Creeper 的程序在阿帕网上爬行，显示“我是爬行者，如果你能抓住我！”

sentences.en: on connected terminals.
sentences.zh: 在连接的终端上。

sentences.en: Another program, Reaper, was unleashed to hunt it down.
sentences.zh: 另一个程序“Reaper”被释放来追捕它。

blocks.html_en: Only about 1,500 PDP-10s were ever sold, but their cultural impact is immeasurable. DEC cancelled the line in 1983, killed internally by the success of its own VAX architecture. But the spirit of the PDP-10 lives on in hacker culture.

sentences.en: Only about 1,500 PDP-10s were ever sold, but their cultural impact is immeasurable.
sentences.zh: PDP-10 仅售出约 1,500 台，但其文化影响却是不可估量的。

sentences.en: DEC cancelled the line in 1983, killed internally by the success of its own VAX architecture.
sentences.zh: DEC 于 1983 年取消了该生产线，并因其自己的 VAX 架构的成功而在内部被终止。

sentences.en: But the spirit of the PDP-10 lives on in hacker culture.
sentences.zh: 但 PDP-10 的精神在黑客文化中依然存在。

blocks.html_en: 7. PDP-11 — Defining Normal

sentences.en: PDP-11 — Defining Normal
sentences.zh: PDP-11 — 定义正常

blocks.html_en: In 1970, DEC launched a machine that would change everything. The PDP-11 was a radical break. It was a 16-bit machine with an orthogonal instruction set that made it far easier to program than anything before it. It had eight general-purpose registers (later models had more). It introduced the Unibus, a standardized bus that made adding peripherals simple. And the design scaled up from a tiny 4K embedded controller to a system with 8 megabytes that could rival mainframes — a scale factor of 2,000.

sentences.en: In 1970, DEC launched a machine that would change everything.
sentences.zh: 1970 年，DEC 推出了一台改变一切的机器。

sentences.en: The PDP-11 was a radical break.
sentences.zh: PDP-11 是一次彻底的突破。

sentences.en: It was a 16-bit machine with an orthogonal instruction set that made it far easier to program than anything before it.
sentences.zh: 它是一台具有正交指令集的 16 位机器，使得编程比之前的任何机器都容易得多。

sentences.en: It had eight general-purpose registers (later models had more).
sentences.zh: 它有八个通用寄存器（后来的型号有更多）。

sentences.en: It introduced the Unibus, a standardized bus that made adding peripherals simple.
sentences.zh: 它引入了 Unibus，这是一种标准化总线，可以让添加外设变得简单。

sentences.en: And the design scaled up from a tiny 4K embedded controller to a system with 8 megabytes that could rival mainframes — a scale factor of 2,000.
sentences.zh: 该设计从微型 4K 嵌入式控制器扩展到可与大型机相媲美的 8 MB 系统——比例因子为 2,000。

blocks.html_en: The design was so elegant that every major microprocessor architecture that came after — the Intel x86, the Motorola 68000 — was visibly shaped by it. The 68000's register set, the x86's addressing modes, the very idea of what a CPU should look like: the PDP-11 defined it.

sentences.en: The design was so elegant that every major microprocessor architecture that came after — the Intel x86, the Motorola 68000 — was visibly shaped by it.
sentences.zh: 该设计非常优雅，以至于后来的每一个主要微处理器架构——英特尔 x86、摩托罗拉 68000——都明显受到了它的影响。

sentences.en: The 68000's register set, the x86's addressing modes, the very idea of what a CPU should look like: the PDP-11 defined it.
sentences.zh: 68000 的寄存器组、x86 的寻址模式、CPU 的基本概念：PDP-11 定义了它。

blocks.html_en: Where Unix Grew Up

sentences.en: Where Unix Grew Up
sentences.zh: Unix 成长的地方

blocks.html_en: In 1970, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs ported their experimental operating system — Unix — to the PDP-11/20. It was the first machine Unix ran on as a named operating system. Over the next decade, Unix and the PDP-11 evolved together. The C programming language was designed specifically to be efficient on the PDP-11's architecture. The abstract machine that C targets, to this day, is a PDP-11 in its fundamental assumptions.

sentences.en: In 1970, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs ported their experimental operating system — Unix — to the PDP-11/20.
sentences.zh: 1970 年，贝尔实验室的 Ken Thompson 和 Dennis Ritchie 将他们的实验操作系统 Unix 移植到了 PDP-11/20 上。

sentences.en: It was the first machine Unix ran on as a named operating system.
sentences.zh: 它是第一台运行 Unix 作为命名操作系统的机器。

sentences.en: Over the next decade, Unix and the PDP-11 evolved together.
sentences.zh: 在接下来的十年里，Unix 和 PDP-11 共同发展。

sentences.en: The C programming language was designed specifically to be efficient on the PDP-11's architecture.
sentences.zh: C 编程语言专门设计用于在 PDP-11 架构上高效运行。

sentences.en: The abstract machine that C targets, to this day, is a PDP-11 in its fundamental assumptions.
sentences.zh: 迄今为止，C 语言所针对的抽象机器的基本假设仍然是 PDP-11。

blocks.html_en: The PDP-11's influence is even visible in the syntax of C itself. The close relationship between arrays and pointers in C — the fact that array[i] is equivalent to *(array + i) — is not an accident of language design. It reflects the PDP-11's architecture, where memory addressing was uniform and efficient. C was not designed for an abstract machine; it was designed for the PDP-11.

sentences.en: The PDP-11's influence is even visible in the syntax of C itself.
sentences.zh: PDP-11 的影响甚至在 C 语言本身的语法中也可见一斑。

sentences.en: The close relationship between arrays and pointers in C — the fact that array[i] is equivalent to *(array + i) — is not an accident of language design.
sentences.zh: C 中数组和指针之间的密切关系（事实上 array[i] 相当于 *(array + i)）并不是语言设计的偶然。

sentences.en: It reflects the PDP-11's architecture, where memory addressing was uniform and efficient.
sentences.zh: 它反映了 PDP-11 的架构，其中内存寻址是统一且高效的。

sentences.en: C was not designed for an abstract machine; it was designed for the PDP-11.
sentences.zh: C 不是为抽象机设计的；它是为 PDP-11 设计的。

blocks.html_en: The Unix source code for the PDP-11 contains one of the most famous comments in programming history. In the I/O driver for the 11/20, Ken Thompson wrote: "You are not expected to understand this". It was a joke about the complexity of the interrupt system, but it became legendary.

sentences.en: The Unix source code for the PDP-11 contains one of the most famous comments in programming history.
sentences.zh: PDP-11 的 Unix 源代码包含编程历史上最著名的注释之一。

sentences.en: In the I/O driver for the 11/20, Ken Thompson wrote: "You are not expected to understand this".
sentences.zh: 在 11/20 的 I/O 驱动程序中，Ken Thompson 写道：“你不应该理解这一点”。

sentences.en: It was a joke about the complexity of the interrupt system, but it became legendary.
sentences.zh: 这是关于中断系统复杂性的一个笑话，但却成为传奇。

blocks.html_en: When you open a terminal on a modern Linux or macOS system, you are in a direct line of descent from a programmer sitting at a PDP-11 in 1971. The file system hierarchy, the pipe operator, the shell itself — all of it was invented on the PDP-11.

sentences.en: When you open a terminal on a modern Linux or macOS system, you are in a direct line of descent from a programmer sitting at a PDP-11 in 1971.
sentences.zh: 当你在现代 Linux 或 macOS 系统上打开终端时，你就是 1971 年坐在 PDP-11 前的程序员的直系血统。

sentences.en: The file system hierarchy, the pipe operator, the shell itself — all of it was invented on the PDP-11.
sentences.zh: 文件系统层次结构、管道操作符、shell 本身——所有这些都是在 PDP-11 上发明的。

blocks.html_en: The Road Not Taken — RSX-11

sentences.en: The Road Not Taken — RSX-11
sentences.zh: 未选择的路 — RSX-11

blocks.html_en: But Unix was not the only operating system on the PDP-11, and in fact it was DEC's least favorite. The company's own RSX-11M was a groundbreaking multi-user, real-time OS that feels utterly different from Unix. But its integrated development environment, its seamless multitasking, its approach to resource management — RSX was an alternative vision of computing that could have won. Easily.

sentences.en: But Unix was not the only operating system on the PDP-11, and in fact it was DEC's least favorite.
sentences.zh: 但 Unix 并不是 PDP-11 上唯一的操作系统，事实上它也是 DEC 最不喜欢的操作系统。

sentences.en: The company's own RSX-11M was a groundbreaking multi-user, real-time OS that feels utterly different from Unix.
sentences.zh: 该公司自己的 RSX-11M 是一个突破性的多用户实时操作系统，感觉与 Unix 完全不同。

sentences.en: But its integrated development environment, its seamless multitasking, its approach to resource management — RSX was an alternative vision of computing that could have won.
sentences.zh: 但它的集成开发环境、无缝多任务处理、资源管理方法——RSX 是一种可能获胜的另类计算愿景。

sentences.en: Easily.
sentences.zh: 容易地。

blocks.html_en: Here is where the story takes a strange turn. When Microsoft decided to break with the MS-DOS past in the late 1980s, Dave Cutler, the lead architect of RSX-11M (and later of DEC's VMS), was tasked with building a new operating system from scratch. That became Windows NT. Its kernel design, its I/O model, and its structured exception handling all bear the marks of the PDP-11 RSX heritage. So: the other half of the modern desktop, the non-Unix half, also traces back to the PDP-11.

sentences.en: Here is where the story takes a strange turn.
sentences.zh: 故事在这里发生了奇怪的转折。

sentences.en: When Microsoft decided to break with the MS-DOS past in the late 1980s, Dave Cutler, the lead architect of RSX-11M (and later of DEC's VMS), was tasked with building a new operating system from scratch.

blocks.html_en: In October 1972, ARPA organized a public demonstration at the International Conference on Computer Communication in Washington, D.C. content_html_zh:
计算如何摆脱批处理并变得个人化。 通过使故事发生的机器来讲述故事。

大多数人会提到 ENIAC 或 IBM System/360 作为早期计算机的例子。 房间填充机器由打孔卡供电，产生工资单运行和科学计算。 是的，这是故事的一个重要部分——但这不是我们的故事。 我们在日常生活中实际使用的计算机很早就脱离了这条道路。

除了大型机之外，另一种不同的计算方式正在形成。 您可以将计算机用作您可以坐下来进行交互的工具。 您无需等待批处理作业返回几个小时。 这就是导致 Windows、Linux、Android、口袋里的智能手机的诞生的原因。 以及洗碗机中的微控制器。

本页是对该故事的介绍。 它涵盖了关键的机器和一些人。 它想要告诉我们的计算机及其背后的基本思想来自哪里。

我们承认：这是我们的观点。 我们保证过时，我们的目标是通过我们制作的复制品亲自体验这些机器。 对于任何疏忽或偏见，我们深表歉意。 我们无能为力，我们喜欢我们的偏见。

序言：阿兰·图灵

在计算机出现之前，存在一个问题：什么是计算？ 1936年，当时24岁的剑桥数学家艾伦·图灵通过一个思想实验回答了这个问题。 一台虚构的机器，可以按照简单的规则在无限的磁带上读取和写入符号。 原则上，“通用图灵机”可以执行任何计算机可以执行的任何计算。 这是一个纯粹的理论构造，但定义了可能性的边界。

十年后，图灵在布莱切利公园建造了真正的机器来破解德国恩尼格玛密码。 炸弹（以及后来的巨像）是特殊用途的设备，但证明了电子计算的实用性。 图灵本人继续在国家物理实验室设计了 ACE（自动计算引擎），这是最早的存储程序计算机之一。

图灵对交互式计算的影响是根本性的。 他证明机器可以是通用的。 不仅仅是一个计算器，更是一个思考的工具。

图灵的想法不是理论性的。 Pilot ACE 于 1950 年在国家物理实验室建造，是世界上最快的计算机：处理速度约为 1 MHz，这在当时是惊人的速度。 1950 年，图灵发表了另一篇开创性论文——《计算机器与智能》——提出了一个看似简单的问题：机器能思考吗？ 他提出了模仿游戏，现在被称为图灵测试。 这个问题仍然没有答案，但交互式计算正是它值得一问的原因。

1. 旋风计划——第一台交互式计算机

1945年，美国海军要求麻省理工学院建造一个更好的飞行模拟器。 他们想要一台能够实时模拟飞机的机器，能够足够快地计算空气动力，以便飞行员可以凭感觉驾驶它。 这是一个完全疯狂的要求。 从来没有一台计算机能够以人类的速度运行。 这成为了一次非常成功的失败。

负责这项工作的麻省理工学院年轻工程师杰伊·福雷斯特 (Jay Forrester) 并不知道这是不可能的。 他建造了旋风。 1951 年的跑步是一个启示。 它有一个 CRT 显示器，你可以观看它绘制矢量。 它有一个光笔、用于直接输入的开关和按钮：第一台设计用于与人类实时交互的计算机。 这个时代的所有其他计算机都运行批处理作业：交出一堆打孔卡，稍后再回来。 旋风坐在那里跟你顶嘴。

一路走来，福雷斯特和他的团队发明了磁芯存储器。 穿有电线的铁氧体环可以保存数据（实际上，即使没有电源）。 二十年来，核心内存一直是占主导地位的随机存取内存技术，并且至今仍在一些航天器中使用。 它的诞生是因为《旋风》中的真空管内存不断失效，而 Forrester 需要一些可靠的东西。

Whirlwind 是一个庞然大物：有 12,500 个真空管，消耗 150 kW 的功率，但每秒只能管理 20,000 次操作。 但在这个项目中，一些更小但更重要的东西正在形成。 内存测试计算机 (MTC) 是为了测试 Forrester 的新核心内存而构建的，其中一位从事该工作的工程师是一位年轻的麻省理工学院毕业生，名叫肯·奥尔森 (Ken Olsen)。 MTC 教会了奥尔森后来构建 DEC 所需的一切。

Whirlwind 的子系统 SAGE 防空系统进一步推动了交互式计算的发展。 SAGE 操作员坐在大型 CRT 显示器前，用光枪瞄准飞机上的光点——这是鼠标和随后的所有触摸屏的直接祖先。

旋风从未成功完成飞行模拟器的角色；它被重定向到空域防御，监听雷达站并指挥拦截机。 这直接导致了 SAGE 防空系统的诞生。 更重要的是，它造就了麻省理工学院林肯实验室的一代工程师，他们从经验中知道，计算机可以做比批处理更有趣的事情。

2. TX-0 — 晶体管到货

Whirlwind 证明了交互式计算的可能性，但填满了一座大型建筑并消耗了 150 kW 的电力。 下一步是让它更小、更便宜、更方便。 这意味着用晶体管取代真空管。

TX-0（“零晶体管实验计算机”，亲切地称为“tixo”）是于 1955 年至 1956 年间在林肯实验室制造的。 这是第一台完全晶体管化的计算机，使用大约 3,600 个 Philco 表面势垒晶体管。 它拥有当时巨大的 64K 18 位字核心内存，而且最重要的是，它还有一个控制台。 您可以坐在 TX-0 前并直接与它交互。

这是麻省理工学院的技术模型铁路俱乐部发现的机器。 TMRC 成员已经习惯了为他们的模型火车构建复杂的信号系统，当他们使用 TX-0 时，他们发现了一种新的游乐场。 他们编写程序，试验显示器，并将机器推向其设计者从未想象过的方向。 他们是第一批“黑客”——这个词在 TMRC 中已经存在，用于描述精心设计的、创造性的恶作剧或项目——他们将这种精神带入了计算领域。

“黑客”一词并非起源于计算机。 在 TMRC 中，“黑客”是针对技术挑战的一种创造性的、通常很有趣的解决方案——为模型火车连接复杂的信号系统就是一种黑客。 当俱乐部成员将这种心态转移到 TX-0 上时，这个词找到了它真正的归宿。 黑客仍然保留着最初的含义：不是破坏者，而是热爱机器的创造性问题解决者。

从某种意义上说，TX-0 从来就只是一块垫脚石。 它是作为更大的 TX-2（由 Wesley Clark 设计的 36 位机器）的测试平台而构建的。 当麻省理工学院于 1960 年获得第一台 PDP-1 时，TX-0 悄然退役——最终送给了一家博物馆。 它的遗产不是机器本身，而是它培养的一代工程师和程序员。

曾参与 Whirlwind 内存测试计算机工作的麻省理工学院工程师肯·奥尔森 (Ken Olsen) 指导了 TX-0 的构建。 他看到了事情的发展方向：计算机可以成为个人工具。

3. 数字设备公司

1957 年，来自麻省理工学院林肯实验室的奥尔森和哈兰·安德森决定创办一家公司。 他们从乔治·多里奥特的美国研究与开发公司获得了 70,000 美元的风险投资；历史上最早的风险投资交易之一。 他们在马萨诸塞州梅纳德大街 146 号的一栋 19 世纪旧磨坊大楼里开设了商店。

公司名称是经过精心选择的。 1957 年，IBM 制造了“计算机”——用于企业数据中心的巨型、令人生畏的机器。 没有风险投资家会资助另一家计算机公司。 因此奥尔森和安德森将其称为“数字设备公司”：“数字”听起来很安全，“设备”听起来很工业，而名称中没有“计算机”。

他们的第一个产品是用于测试其他系统的逻辑模块。 但奥尔森有更大的想法。 TX-0 之后是 TX-2，这是由 Wesley Clark 设计的更大的 36 位机器。 Olsen 吸取了 TX-0 和 TX-2 的教训，问道：如果我们能够制造一台机器，将交互式计算带出实验室，带到现实世界，会怎样？

奥尔森后来成为计算机界最受引用的人物之一。 他最著名的一句话——“任何人都没有理由在家里拥有一台电脑”（1977 年）——几乎总是被断章取义。 他指的是用于控制家用电器的计算机，而不是刚刚出现的个人计算机。 奥尔森本人家里就有一台 PDP-11。 这句话在他余下的职业生涯中一直困扰着他，但这反映出即使是最有远见的领导者也很难预测交互式计算的下一步发展。

4. PDP-1——这一切的开始

1959 年，DEC 发布了 PDP-1——编程数据处理器-1。 它的成本为 12 万美元，大约是 IBM 大型机价格的十分之一。 它有 4,096 个字的 18 位核心内存、27 条指令和一个由大约 2,700 个晶体管组成的中央处理器。 与那个时代充满房间的 IBM 机器相比，它看起来就像一个玩具。 虽然只生产了 54 台，但这 54 台机器确实改变了世界。

PDP-1 拥有 IBM 机器所没有的东西：Type 30 显示屏。 这是一个改装的雷达管。 显示器直接从处理器的 I/O 寄存器中获取位作为 X/Y 坐标，并将它们绘制在荧光屏上。 这是最简单的图形子系统。 它不需要图形内存，但这意味着必须不断重新绘制图像。 尽管如此，这正是交互式计算所需要的。

太空战争！

1962 年，一群麻省理工学院的学生——Steve Russell、Martin Graetz 和 Wayne Wiitanen——在 PDP-1 上编写了一个游戏。 两艘由不同组开关控制的宇宙飞船在围绕一颗恒星运行时互相发射鱼雷。 他们称之为太空战争！ 这是第一个数字视频游戏。

太空战争！ 有重力、推力力学，还有一颗恒星，如果你不小心，它就会把你拉进去并摧毁你。 它还拥有有史以来第一个视频游戏控制器：一对由同学 Alan Kotok 制作的定制开关盒，他从 DEC 本身获得了零件清单。 该游戏是免费发行的，每个 PDP-1 网站最终都有一份。 这是第一个病毒式传播的软件。

PDP-1 也是第一台在公共场合演奏音乐的计算机。 在麻省理工学院 1963 年的科学开放日上，Harmony 音乐编译器通过连接到机器输出寄存器的无线电扬声器播放旋律。 这是计算机音乐的早期开端，并证明即使使用 4K 内存，您也可以创作艺术。

“黑客”从何而来

麻省理工学院的 PDP-1 社区（其中许多人来自 TMRC）从模型铁路俱乐部中汲取了“黑客”一词，并将其应用到编程中。 hack 是一种优雅且富有创意的解决方案。 PDP-1 是黑客的完美机器：足够简单以完全理解，足够互动以提供即时反馈，并且足够有限以要求创造力。

当 IBM 程序员编写代码、将其提交给按键操作员并在一天后获得结果时，PDP-1 黑客坐在控制台前，切换指令，立即观看结果。 这种即时性是革命性的。 它改变了人们对计算机的看法。

首例数不胜数，无法一一列举

PDP-1 创造了数量惊人的软件第一。 第一个文本编辑器。 几乎第一个交互式调试器（DDT，动态调试技术）。 第一个分时操作系统，允许多个用户同时工作。 Peter Deutsch，一名高中生，将 Lisp 移植到了 PDP-1，并在此过程中发明了读取-评估-打印循环——REPL，现在是 Python、Ruby 和每个交互式编程环境的基础。 但 PDP-1 首先是解码和游戏的诞生地：

5. PDP-8 — 光荣的极简主义

PDP-1 已经证明交互式计算在商业上是可行的。 但 DEC 意识到，为了进入更广阔的市场，他们需要一台足够便宜的机器，用于单个实验室或工厂车间。 因此，他们将 PDP-1 概念剥离至其本质。

PDP-8 于 1965 年推出，是将 PDP-1 的 18 位架构缩减为 12 位。 指令集从 27 条减少到 8 条。 内存为 4,096 个 12 位字，程序员一次只能直接寻址 128 个字——其他一切都需要页面切换技巧。 它的价格不到 20,000 美元，使其成为第一台单个部门无需公司批准即可购买的计算机。

DEC 认为 PDP-8 将是一个工业控制器。 当压力过高时打开阀门。 当温度升高时停止加热器。 他们不知道自己即将发明个人计算机。

DEC 的首席工程师戈登·贝尔 (Gordon Bell) 将 PDP-8 称为“计算领域的 T 型”，这种比较是恰当的。 正如福特的装配线让汽车变得更便宜一样，PDP-8 让计算机变得触手可及。 正如 T 型车催生了整个零部件和服务行业一样，PDP-8 创建了小型机生态系统。

PDP-8 的 OS/8 操作系统是 CP/M 的直接祖先，而 CP/M 又是 MS-DOS 的直接祖先。 每台 PC 的软件 DNA 都可以追溯到这个血统。 1968 年，OS/8 运行在一台安装在机架式机箱中、具有 4K 内存的机器上。

值得注意的是，PDP-8 还运行 TSS/8，这是一种分时操作系统，可以让四个用户同时访问该机器。 在具有 8 条指令和 4K 字内存的计算机上。 如果这听起来不可能，那么——这正是重点。 PDP-8 迫使程序员成为天才，因为它没有给他们提供其他可以使用的东西。

PDP-8 在其生命周期内已售出超过 50,000 台。 它是个人计算机和微控制器的原型/鼻祖。

6. PDP-10 — 使用起来确实很有趣的主机

当 PDP-8 征服低端市场时，DEC 正在开发一些完全不同的高端产品。 1964 年的 PDP-6 引入了具有丰富指令集的 36 位架构，但现在对现代程序员来说完全陌生。 但 PDP-6 并不可靠。 当 DEC 正确使用 PDP-10（KA10，1968）时，其结果与计算领域的其他任何结果都不同。

PDP-10 是一个大型机——它很大，很昂贵（超过 100,000 美元），而且功能强大。 但与同时代的其他大型机不同，它是为交互式使用而设计的。 没有批处理。 你坐在终端前，机器回答你。 这就是 PDP-10 的特殊之处。

麻省理工学院人工智能实验室和 ITS

在麻省理工学院的人工智能实验室，PDP-10 运行一个名为 ITS 的操作系统——不兼容分时系统。 ITS 是黑客的天堂：没有密码，没有安全保障。 但早期阿帕网上的任何人都可以登录。 他们做到了。

ITS 是 Emacs 的诞生地（Richard Stallman，1976）。 MacLisp 在这里成长，开创了许多现代编程语言设计的先河。 Shrdlu——第一个能够理解三维世界并遵守英语命令的人工智能程序——让参观者眼花缭乱。 Mazewar 成为第一款网络多人第一人称射击游戏，通过新兴的 ARPANET 连接 PDP-10。

可以毫不夸张地说，现代计算机科学是在PDP-10上锻造出来的。 自由软件运动始于斯托曼对黑客社区商业化的反应。 PDP-10 在早期的 ARPANET 中占据主导地位。 顺便说一句，比尔·盖茨和保罗·艾伦使用他们自己编写的 8080 模拟器在哈佛 PDP-10 上编写了第一个 Microsoft BASIC。 开源和微软诞生在同一个系统上！

PDP-10 还见证了第一个计算机蠕虫病毒。 20 世纪 70 年代初，一个名为 Creeper 的程序在阿帕网上爬行，显示“我是爬行者，如果你能抓住我！” 在连接的终端上。 另一个程序“Reaper”被释放来追捕它。

PDP-10 仅售出约 1,500 台，但其文化影响却是不可估量的。 DEC 于 1983 年取消了该生产线，并因其自己的 VAX 架构的成功而在内部被终止。 但 PDP-10 的精神在黑客文化中依然存在。

7. PDP-11 — 定义正常

1970 年，DEC 推出了一台改变一切的机器。 PDP-11 是一次彻底的突破。 它是一台具有正交指令集的 16 位机器，使得编程比之前的任何机器都容易得多。 它有八个通用寄存器（后来的型号有更多）。 它引入了 Unibus，这是一种标准化总线，可以让添加外设变得简单。 该设计从微型 4K 嵌入式控制器扩展到可与大型机相媲美的 8 MB 系统——比例因子为 2,000。

该设计非常优雅，以至于后来的每一个主要微处理器架构——英特尔 x86、摩托罗拉 68000——都明显受到了它的影响。 68000 的寄存器组、x86 的寻址模式、CPU 的基本概念：PDP-11 定义了它。

Unix 成长的地方

1970 年，贝尔实验室的 Ken Thompson 和 Dennis Ritchie 将他们的实验操作系统 Unix 移植到了 PDP-11/20 上。 它是第一台运行 Unix 作为命名操作系统的机器。 在接下来的十年里，Unix 和 PDP-11 共同发展。 C 编程语言专门设计用于在 PDP-11 架构上高效运行。 迄今为止，C 语言所针对的抽象机器的基本假设仍然是 PDP-11。

PDP-11 的影响甚至在 C 语言本身的语法中也可见一斑。 C 中数组和指针之间的密切关系（事实上 array[i] 相当于 *(array + i)）并不是语言设计的偶然。 它反映了 PDP-11 的架构，其中内存寻址是统一且高效的。 C 不是为抽象机设计的；它是为 PDP-11 设计的。

PDP-11 的 Unix 源代码包含编程历史上最著名的注释之一。 在 11/20 的 I/O 驱动程序中，Ken Thompson 写道：“你不应该理解这一点”。 这是关于中断系统复杂性的一个笑话，但却成为传奇。

当你在现代 Linux 或 macOS 系统上打开终端时，你就是 1971 年坐在 PDP-11 前的程序员的直系血统。 文件系统层次结构、管道操作符、shell 本身——所有这些都是在 PDP-11 上发明的。

未选择的路 — RSX-11

但 Unix 并不是 PDP-11 上唯一的操作系统，事实上它也是 DEC 最不喜欢的操作系统。 该公司自己的 RSX-11M 是一个突破性的多用户实时操作系统，感觉与 Unix 完全不同。 但它的集成开发环境、无缝多任务处理、资源管理方法——RSX 是一种可能获胜的另类计算愿景。 容易地。

故事在这里发生了奇怪的转折。 当 Microsoft 在 20 世纪 80 年代末决定与过去的 MS-DOS 决裂时，RSX-11M（以及后来的 DEC VMS）的首席架构师 Dave Cutler 的任务是从头开始构建一个新的操作系统。 这就是Windows NT。 其内核设计、I/O 模型以及结构化异常处理都带有 PDP-11 RSX 传统的印记。 所以：现代桌面的另一半，即非 Unix 的一半，也可以追溯到 PDP-11。

售出超过 600,000 台 PDP-11。 它们被用于实验室、工厂、大学、电话交换机和航天器。 顶级 PDP-11/70 凭借第二个 MASSBUS 接口进一步提升了性能，能够以每秒 4 兆字节的速度传输数据，这在 1975 年是惊人的速度。 该架构已持续生产超过 25 年。 当您使用任何现代计算机（PC、Mac 或 Linux 工作站）时，您都在遵循 PDP-11 设计者在 20 世纪 60 年代末做出的决定。

8. 阿帕网——一切相连的地方

到 20 世纪 60 年代末，问题不再是计算能力，而是隔离。 美国各地的研究实验室拥有功能强大的交互式计算机，但每个实验室都是一座孤岛。 如果您在麻省理工学院人工智能实验室开发 PDP-10，并想使用在斯坦福大学机器上运行的程序，那么您就可以开车了。

答案来自高级研究计划局 (ARPA)，该机构是五角大楼的一个机构，一直为计算机科学研究提供大部分资金。 1968 年，ARPA 发出了建设实验性分组交换网络的征求建议书。 该合同颁给了博尔特、贝拉内克和纽曼 (BBN)，这是一家位于马萨诸塞州剑桥的公司，由两位麻省理工学院的教授创立。 BBN 拥有深厚的 DEC 专业知识——他们拥有多台 PDP-1 和 PDP-10，并且确切地知道如何让计算机相互通信。

让它工作的设备是 IMP——接口消息处理器。 它是一台坚固耐用的小型计算机（最初是霍尼韦尔 DDP-516），位于站点的主计算机和电话线之间。 它的工作是从本地计算机接收消息，将它们分成数据包，然后通过网络将它们路由到目的地。 IMP 是第一个专用网络路由器，其软件由 BBN 团队编写，其中包括几位前麻省理工学院黑客。

首批四个 ARPANET 节点于 1969 年底上线：加州大学洛杉矶分校、斯坦福研究所、加州大学圣巴巴拉分校和犹他大学。 到 1971 年，已有 15 个。 麻省理工学院很早就加入了，其运行 ITS 的 PDP-10 成为网络最受欢迎的目的地之一——黑客精神与网络相遇的神奇地方。

1971 年，BBN 工程师 Ray Tomlinson 发明了电子邮件。 他选择@符号来分隔用户名和机器名，因为它已经在键盘上并且“有意义”。 电子邮件将成为早期阿帕网的杀手级应用程序——@符号仍然存在。

1972 年：演示改变了一切

1972 年 10 月，ARPA 在华盛顿特区举行的国际计算机通信会议上组织了一次公开演示。 在三天的时间里，与会者可以坐在与全国 10 个地点的计算机相连的 40 个终端之一（叮当作响的电传打字机和时尚的新型 CRT 终端）与全国各地的计算机连接。 他们可以登录麻省理工学院的 PDP-10，在斯坦福人工智能实验室的机器上运行程序，向剑桥的 BBN PDP-10 发送消息。 网络起作用了。 人们看到它起作用了。

这是互联网从研究项目变成必然的时刻。 1972 年演示中的终端通过 IMP 连接，IMP 通过租用的电话线完全自动地路由流量。 该技术是自组织的——IMP 会宣布其存在，了解其邻居，并且在几秒钟内整个网络都知道了它。 这一设计原则经过数十年的完善，至今仍然是互联网的运作方式。

阿帕网在 20 世纪 70 年代迅速发展。 PDP-10 是其早期的骨干——运行早期网络服务、托管第一批电子邮件服务器并构成互联网核心的机器。 到 1977 年，该网络已发展成为横跨整个大陆的网络。

目前，我们正在构建 IMP 的复制品，作为更大的阿帕网重建项目的一部分，旨在重建 1972-73 年的网络供冲浪。 这是拼图的最后一块，将这个故事中的所有机器连接在一起。

回顾过去

交互式计算的故事不仅仅与硬件有关。 这也与人们对计算机用途的转变有关。 旋风证明计算机可以实时响应人类。 TX-0 和麻省理工学院的黑客证明了交互式访问可以孕育创造力。 DEC 的业务围绕着制造计算机个人工具而非机构大型机展开。

这些机器中的每一个都建立在之前的机器的基础上，但它们的发展并不顺利。 PDP-8 是一种有意的简化，但使计算变得更加容易。 它是早期个人计算机和微控制器的根源。 PDP-10 进入了大型机领域，但怀着一颗黑客的心。 现代软件的诞生地，尽管硬件本身实际上是一条死胡同。 PDP-11 是从头开始的重新思考，它在很多方面都是正确的，它是第一台“普通”计算机 - 它定义了我们今天使用的计算机。

到 20 世纪 80 年代初，微处理器已经吸收了所有这些机器的经验教训。 交互式计算之战取得了胜利。

但体验这些前辈机器仍然有一些特别之处。 在 PDP-8 前面板上切换引导程序并在加载纸带时观察 Blinkenlights。 坐在 PDP-1 控制台前输入 12 行汇编代码，在雷达管上画一个圆圈。 在 PDP-10 上登录 ITS，并意识到您正在使用与 Richard Stallman 发明 Emacs 时使用的相同操作系统，并且该操作系统搭载了最早的人工智能。

这就是我们副本社区存在的原因。 这些机器不能只是博物馆里死去的文物——它们应该经过亲身实践才能了解计算机的历史。 博物馆可能会向您展示历史。 复制品可以让你活下去。
